prerequisites: Distinguish a topic from a statement about that topic.
Recognize words marking contrast or limitation, such as but, some and before.
Use only what the passage states or supports, not outside assumptions.
explanation: The main idea is the central point made about a topic across the passage. A true detail may be too narrow; an impressive general claim may be unsupported. Identify the situation, what changes or is argued, and why the ending matters. Test your proposed summary against every sentence. Preserve limits such as some, a trial or an undecided outcome.

worked.action: Read this original example: A school opened its courtyard at lunch. Pupils used shaded benches for reading, but the noisy corner remained reserved for games. Staff kept both spaces because pupils wanted different kinds of breaks.
worked.justification: The topic is use of the courtyard, not benches alone.

worked.action: List the roles: opening gives the situation; reading and games give contrasting uses; the final sentence explains keeping both.
worked.justification: A main idea must connect these roles rather than repeat one detail.

worked.action: Choose: The school kept different courtyard spaces to support different lunchtime activities.
worked.justification: This covers reading, games and the decision, with no claim that everyone prefers one activity.

worked.action: Reject: All pupils prefer quiet reading.
worked.justification: This contradicts the reported variety. Rejecting an overstatement is different from rejecting a true but narrow detail such as pupils used benches.

worked.action: For a trial with mixed early evidence, summarize the trial and cautious decision, not a guaranteed future result.
worked.justification: Words such as some, before deciding and not yet preserve the author's degree of certainty.

hint: Say what the passage is mainly doing in one sentence. Check the opening, contrast and ending against that sentence.
shortcut: Use topic plus central point as a draft, then test it against the whole passage.
limitation: The last sentence is useful evidence, not an automatic answer. A title-like topic label alone and a true minor detail can both miss the main idea.

entry.passage: The community library began lending seeds as well as books. Borrowers were asked to return seeds from their harvest if they could. The programme gave neighbours a way to exchange both plants and growing advice.
entry.stem: Passage 1: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the whole passage?
options: A library programme connects neighbours through shared seeds and advice.
Every borrower must return exactly the same number of seeds.
Libraries should replace their books with plants.
The programme proves that all neighbours grow vegetables.
explanations: This includes the programme and its social purpose across all three sentences.
The passage says if they could; it gives no exact number.
Books are still lent; replacement is not proposed.
No universal claim about neighbours or vegetables appears.
repairs: This includes the programme and its social purpose across all three sentences. Reread the beginning and ending, then check whether your summary covers the middle without adding a stronger claim.
The passage says if they could; it gives no exact number. Reread the beginning and ending, then check whether your summary covers the middle without adding a stronger claim.
Books are still lent; replacement is not proposed. Reread the beginning and ending, then check whether your summary covers the middle without adding a stronger claim.
No universal claim about neighbours or vegetables appears. Reread the beginning and ending, then check whether your summary covers the middle without adding a stronger claim.
entry.reason_prompt: Which passage-level evidence supports the summary?
reason_options: The first sentence introduces seed lending; the last explains the exchange it enables.
A memorable single detail is sufficient even when the rest of the passage has a different focus.
A summary should strengthen a limited observation into a rule applying to every case.
A likely consequence may replace what the author actually describes.
entry.reason_explanation: The first sentence introduces seed lending; the last explains the exchange it enables.

revision.passage: An apartment association compared monthly water-meter totals after fitting new taps. Consumption fell, but several flats had also been empty that month. The committee recorded both changes and postponed its claim about savings until occupied-flat figures were available. It still kept the new taps in use.
revision.stem: Passage 9: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the whole passage?
options: The committee refused to attribute lower water use solely to new taps while occupancy also changed.
The new taps certainly caused all of the fall in water use.
Empty flats prove that water-saving equipment never works.
Several flats were empty during the month of the water comparison.
explanations: This captures the competing explanation and the committee's cautious decision.
The committee postponed precisely this causal attribution.
A competing explanation does not establish that equipment never works.
This is true but is only the competing explanation; it omits the committee's cautious decision about the taps.

revision.passage: A public square is sometimes praised simply because its paving is new. That is an incomplete test of its value. A beautiful surface offers little comfort if there is nowhere to rest in the heat, and an open entrance offers little access if a step excludes some users. Maintenance, shade and usable routes deserve attention alongside appearance. The question is not whether a square looks renewed, but whether people can use it comfortably over time.
revision.stem: Passage 10: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the whole passage?
options: New paving can improve the appearance of a public square.
Public squares should be judged by sustained usability as well as appearance.
Some entrances have steps that restrict access.
Appearance has no value in any public place.
explanations: The opening refers to praise for new paving, but appearance alone is the limited test the author challenges.
This states the argument joining comfort, access and maintenance to appearance.
This is a supported example but misses the wider argument about how to judge a square.
The author asks for attention alongside appearance, not its total rejection.
